title: Power of Parliament to amend the Constitution

content.overview: The Basic Structure Doctrine is the supreme judicial check on Parliament’s constituent amending power under Article 368. Formulated by a 13-judge bench in Kesavananda Bharati (1973), it establishes that Parliament can amend any part of the Constitution, including Fundamental Rights, but cannot damage, emasculate, or destroy its basic structure or constitutional identity.
content.glance: The Basic Structure Doctrine is the supreme judicial check on Parliament’s constituent amending power under Article 368. Formulated by a 13-judge bench in Kesavananda Bharati (1973), it establishes that Parliament can amend any part of the Constitution, including Fundamental Rights, but cannot damage, emasculate, or destroy its basic structure or constitutional identity.
content.study:
Topic at a Glance
The Basic Structure Doctrine is a central feature of Indian constitutional jurisprudence governing the limits of the constituent amending power. It resolves the existential tension between parliamentary sovereignty and constitutional supremacy, establishing that while Parliament has the power to amend the Constitution under Article 368, it does not possess the power to rewrite, destroy, or repeal the Constitution’s foundational identity.

The Historical Clashes Leading to Kesavananda Bharati
1. Shankari Prasad v. Union of India (AIR 1951 SC 458):
   - Challenge to the 1st Constitutional Amendment Act, 1951 (inserting Articles 31A, 31B, and the Ninth Schedule).
   - A unanimous 5-judge bench held that Parliament’s amending power under Article 368 is plenary and unlimited, extending to Part III Fundamental Rights.
   - The word “law” in Article 13(2) refers to ordinary legislative law, not to constituent amendments made under Article 368.
2. Sajjan Singh v. State of Rajasthan (AIR 1965 SC 845):
   - Challenge to the 17th Amendment. The 5-judge bench reaffirmed Shankari Prasad by a 3:2 majority.
   - However, Justice J.R. Mudholkar (borrowing from Pakistani jurist A.K. Brohi and German scholar Carl Schmitt) raised a prophetic doubt: does the Constitution not possess basic features that cannot be abrogated by amendment? Justice Hidayatullah also doubted the absolute power to extinguish fundamental freedoms.
3. I.C. Golaknath v. State of Punjab (AIR 1967 SC 1643):
   - An 11-judge bench, by a 6:5 majority led by Chief Justice Subba Rao, dramatically reversed Shankari Prasad and Sajjan Singh.
   - Held: An amendment under Article 368 is “law” within the meaning of Article 13(2). Therefore, Parliament cannot abridge or take away any Fundamental Right.
   - The Court invoked the American doctrine of Prospective Overruling so that past amendments (1st, 4th, 17th) remained valid, but future abridgments of Part III were barred.
4. The Parliamentary Counter-Attack (24th Amendment, 1971):
   - To nullify Golaknath, Parliament enacted the 24th Amendment:
     (a) Amended Article 13 by adding clause (4): “Nothing in this article shall apply to any amendment of this Constitution made under article 368.”
     (b) Amended Article 368 to declare that Parliament exercises “constituent power” to amend by way of addition, variation, or repeal any provision.

The Watershed: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) 4 SCC 225
A historic 13-judge bench heard the matter for 68 days and delivered an 11-opinion, 703-page judgment by a 7:6 majority on 24 April 1973:
1. Overruled Golaknath: The Court unanimously upheld the 24th Amendment, holding that “law” in Article 13 does not include a constitutional amendment under Article 368, and that Article 368 contains the substantive power to amend Fundamental Rights.
2. Formulated the Basic Structure Limitation:
   The majority (Chief Justice Sikri, Justices Hegde, Mukherjea, Shelat, Grover, Jaganmohan Reddy, and Khanna) held that the word “amend” implies that the original Constitution must survive in identity. Parliament’s constituent power is not a power to destroy the Constitution. Parliament cannot damage or destroy the “Basic Structure” of the Constitution.

The Post-Kesavananda Consolidation & Case Law Ratios
1. Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975) Supp SCC 1:
   - First application of the doctrine to strike down a constitutional amendment.
   - Parliament enacted the 39th Amendment (Article 329A(4)), placing the election of the Prime Minister beyond judicial review.
   - The Supreme Court struck down Article 329A(4) as violative of the Basic Structure: Free and fair elections, Rule of Law, and Judicial Review.
2. Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India (1980) 3 SCC 625:
   - Parliament enacted the 42nd Amendment, inserting clauses (4) and (5) into Article 368 to declare that there are no limitations whatsoever on constituent power and barring judicial review of amendments.
   - The Supreme Court struck down Article 368(4) and (5). Chief Justice Chandrachud held:
     (a) A limited amending power is itself a basic feature of the Constitution; Parliament cannot convert a limited power into an unlimited one.
     (b) Harmony and balance between Fundamental Rights (Part III) and Directive Principles (Part IV) is part of the basic structure.
3. Waman Rao v. Union of India (1981) 2 SCC 362:
   - Established the cut-off date: 24 April 1973 (the date of Kesavananda judgment).
   - Laws placed in the Ninth Schedule on or before 24 April 1973 enjoy constitutional immunity; laws inserted after that date are subject to judicial review for violating the Basic Structure.
4. I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu (2007) 2 SCC 1:
   - A unanimous 9-judge bench reaffirmed Waman Rao. Any post-1973 Ninth Schedule law that violates Fundamental Rights forming part of the Basic Structure (Articles 14, 19, 21) will be struck down using the “Rights Test” and “Essence of the Right Test”.
5. Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association (NJAC Case, 2015):
   - The 99th Constitutional Amendment establishing the National Judicial Appointments Commission was struck down as unconstitutional; independence of the judiciary is an inviolable facet of the Basic Structure.

Illustrative Pillars of the Basic Structure
The Supreme Court has deliberately avoided an exhaustive definition, but settled pillars include:
1. Supremacy of the Constitution;
2. Republican and Democratic form of government;
3. Secular character of the Constitution (S.R. Bommai);
4. Separation of Powers among Legislature, Executive, and Judiciary;
5. Federal character of the Constitution;
6. Judicial Review under Articles 32 and 226 (L. Chandra Kumar);
7. Independence of the Judiciary (NJAC Case);
8. Free and fair elections (Indira Gandhi);
9. Rule of law and non-arbitrariness (Article 14);
10. The Golden Triangle of Articles 14, 19, and 21;
11. Limited amending power of Parliament (Minerva Mills).

Procedural & Courtroom Anchors (Senior Counsel Checklist)
1. Forum & Jurisdiction:
   - A constitutional amendment may be challenged before a court exercising appropriate constitutional jurisdiction; Articles 32 and 226 provide important writ routes where their respective requirements are satisfied.
   - Article 145(3) requires a minimum five-judge bench in the Supreme Court when a case involves a substantial question of law as to the interpretation of the Constitution. That provision does not impose a five-judge Constitution Bench requirement on High Courts.
2. Grounds of Challenge:
   - The court examines compliance with the constitutional amendment procedure in Article 368, including the special majority and, where the proviso applies, the required State ratification.
   - A substantive challenge may invoke the Basic Structure Doctrine. The analysis asks whether the amendment crosses the constitutional limit on constituent power; it should not be reduced to an exhaustive two-ground formula because the precise grounds depend on the amendment and the constitutional text.
3. Test Applied: The “Rights Test” vs “Essence Test” (I.R. Coelho). Does the amendment abrogate the core identity or essential character of a basic feature?

Current-Law Position & Milestone
The Basic Structure Doctrine remains part of the Supreme Court's constitutional jurisprudence. Article 368's text continues to confer constituent power on Parliament while prescribing the amendment procedure; the doctrine supplies a judicially enforced substantive limitation on that power.

sections.heading: Module 1 — Article 368 and the Nature of Constituent Power
sections.body:
Article 368(1) expressly describes Parliament as exercising constituent power to amend the Constitution by addition, variation or repeal, subject to the procedure laid down in Article 368.
Article 368(2) requires passage in each House by a majority of the total membership and by at least two-thirds of members present and voting. Certain specified constitutional changes additionally require ratification by at least one-half of the State Legislatures.
The Basic Structure Doctrine is not written as a separate clause in Article 368. It is a judicial doctrine derived from the nature of constitutional amendment and constitutional supremacy, beginning with Kesavananda Bharati.

sections.heading: Module 2 — From Shankari Prasad to Kesavananda Bharati
sections.body:
Shankari Prasad and Sajjan Singh treated constitutional amendments differently from ordinary law for Article 13 purposes and accepted Parliament’s power to amend Fundamental Rights.
Golaknath (1967), by a 6:5 majority of an 11-judge bench, took the opposite position on the relationship between Article 13 and constitutional amendments.
Kesavananda Bharati (1973), decided by a 13-judge bench by a 7:6 majority, upheld Parliament’s power to amend any constitutional provision but held that the amending power cannot be used to alter the Constitution’s basic structure.

sections.heading: Module 3 — Basic Features and the Post-Kesavananda Cases
sections.body:
The Supreme Court has not supplied a closed catalogue of basic features. Recognized examples across the cases include constitutional supremacy, republican and democratic government, secularism, federalism, separation of powers, judicial review, judicial independence, rule of law and free and fair elections.
Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain applied the doctrine to invalidate part of the 39th Amendment, including provisions that undermined judicial review and free and fair elections.
Minerva Mills held that the limited nature of the amending power itself is a basic feature and that the balance between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles is constitutionally significant.

sections.heading: Module 4 — Ninth Schedule Review and the Rights Test
sections.body:
Waman Rao identified 24 April 1973, the date of the Kesavananda Bharati judgment, as the relevant cut-off for Ninth Schedule review.
I.R. Coelho (2007) held that laws placed in the Ninth Schedule after that date are not automatically immune from judicial review where their constitutional impact implicates rights forming part of the basic structure.
The Ninth Schedule therefore does not create an absolute bar against constitutional review; the court examines the substance and effect of the challenged law through the constitutional tests applicable to the case.

sections.heading: Module 5 — Amendment Challenge, Evidence and Relief
sections.body:
A constitutional-amendment challenge should identify the exact amending provision, the Article 368 procedure invoked, the constitutional feature allegedly impaired, and the concrete manner in which the amendment is said to alter or destroy that feature.
Where the BSA applies to an evidentiary question, ss. 104–106 concern burdens relating to facts in issue and relevant facts, while s. 109 addresses facts especially within a person’s knowledge. These provisions do not create a special “basic-structure burden” or automatically shift every constitutional issue to the State.
Relief depends on the defect established. A court may sever an invalid provision where severability is legally available, or invalidate the offending constitutional amendment to the extent required by the constitutional analysis.

examples.title: Illustration 1 — Unconstitutional Amendment (Striking Down Clause)
examples.body: Parliament passes a constitutional amendment inserting Article 368(4) and (5), declaring that constitutional amendments shall not be called in question in any court on any ground, thereby eliminating judicial review. The Supreme Court strikes down the clauses as void because judicial review and the limited nature of amending power are essential features of the basic structure (Minerva Mills).

examples.title: Illustration 2 — Valid Constitutional Amendment (Upheld)
examples.body: Parliament enacts the 103rd Constitutional Amendment Act, 2019 providing up to 10% reservation for Economically Weaker Sections (EWS). Petitioners challenge it as breaching the basic structure. The Supreme Court in Janhit Abhiyan (2022) upholds the amendment, holding that affirmative economic classification does not alter or destroy the core equality code of the Constitution.

hypotheticals.question: Examine the constitutional validity of the amendment in light of the Second Judges Case, the NJAC judgment (SCAORA v. Union of India, 2015), and the doctrine of separation of powers.
hypotheticals.analysis:
1. Power under Article 368: While Parliament can amend Articles 124 and 217, it cannot alter the Basic Structure.
2. Is Judicial Independence Basic Structure? In the Second Judges Case (1993) and the NJAC Case (2015), the Supreme Court ruled that the independence of the judiciary and the separation of powers under Article 50 are non-negotiable basic features of the Constitution.
3. Executive Veto: Granting executive nominees a veto over judicial appointments subordinates the judiciary to the executive, destroying judicial independence and the checks-and-balances mechanism.
4. Application to Facts: The amendment undermines the institutional autonomy of the higher judiciary.

rows.left: Parliament has NO power to abridge any FR.
rows.right: Parliament CAN amend FRs, without altering basic structure.

misconceptions.trap: An ordinary municipal statute can be challenged on the ground of violating the Basic Structure Doctrine.
misconceptions.correction: Basic Structure Doctrine applies ONLY to test Constitutional Amendments under Article 368. Ordinary statutes are tested against Part III and legislative competence, not directly against basic structure (State of A.P. v. McDowell).

misconceptions.trap: Kesavananda Bharati held that Fundamental Rights cannot be amended.
misconceptions.correction: Kesavananda overruled Golaknath and held that Fundamental Rights CAN be amended, provided their core essence forming part of the basic structure is not destroyed.

misconceptions.trap: The Ninth Schedule provides unconditional blanket immunity to all laws placed in it.
misconceptions.correction: I.R. Coelho (2007) settled that all laws placed in the Ninth Schedule after 24 April 1973 are open to judicial review on the touchstone of Basic Structure.

questionsAndAnswers.question: Trace the evolution of the Basic Structure Doctrine from Shankari Prasad to Kesavananda Bharati and Minerva Mills.
questionsAndAnswers.answer:
I. ISSUE & CONSTITUTIONAL DILEMMA
Whether Parliament possesses unlimited constituent power under Article 368 to amend any provision of the Constitution, or whether there exist inherent, implied limitations preserving the Constitution's foundational identity.

II. THE EVOLUTIONARY TRAJECTORY
1. Shankari Prasad (1951) & Sajjan Singh (1965):
   The Supreme Court held that Parliament's amending power under Article 368 is plenary and unconstrained. The word "law" in Article 13(2) was held to exclude constitutional amendments.
2. The Golaknath Revolt (1967):
   An 11-judge bench held by a 6:5 majority that an amendment under Article 368 is "law" under Article 13(2). Parliament was stripped of all power to abridge Fundamental Rights.
3. The Watershed: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) 4 SCC 225:
   A 13-judge bench overruled Golaknath by a 7:6 majority:
   (a) Upheld the 24th Amendment: "law" in Art 13 does not include constitutional amendments.
   (b) Formulated Basic Structure: The word "amend" does not mean to destroy or replace. Parliament can amend any provision, including Fundamental Rights, but cannot damage or destroy the "Basic Structure".
4. Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India (1980):
   Struck down Article 368(4) and (5) (inserted by 42nd Amendment). A limited amending power and the balance between Part III and Part IV are themselves basic features.

III. CONCLUSION
The Basic Structure Doctrine permanently established constitutional supremacy over parliamentary supremacy in India. Current through the 106th Amendment (2023).

questionsAndAnswers.question: Critically examine the Basic Structure Doctrine in Indian Constitutional Law. questionsAndAnswers.answer:
I. INTRODUCTION & THE PHILOSOPHICAL CONFLICT
The Basic Structure Doctrine is the crowning glory of Indian constitutional jurisprudence. It resolved the high-stakes constitutional warfare between Parliament and the Judiciary over the nature of constituent power. Inheriting a Westminster system grafted upon a written, supreme Constitution, India faced the dilemma: Does Parliament represent the unfettered sovereign will of the people to remake the constitutional order, or is Parliament merely a creature of the Constitution, subject to its immutable principles?

II. THE GENESIS OF THE DOCTRINE: SHANKARI PRASAD TO GOLAKNATH
1. The Classical Unfettered View:
   In Shankari Prasad (1951) and Sajjan Singh (1965), the Court took a positivistic view. Article 368 was treated as absolute; ordinary law under Article 13 was distinct from constituent law.
2. The Golaknath Over-Correction:
   Alarmed by agrarian land takeovers and amendments to the Ninth Schedule, the 11-judge bench in Golaknath (1967) held that Parliament could not touch Fundamental Rights. This created an unyielding impasse, as progressive socio-economic reforms were obstructed.
3. The Parliamentary Reaction:
   Parliament enacted the 24th, 25th, and 29th Amendments, declaring its constituent power to be unbounded by Article 13 or judicial review.

III. THE KESAVANANDA BHARATI BREAKTHROUGH (1973)
1. The 13-Judge Bench Ruling:
   In Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) 4 SCC 225, the Court delivered a profound compromise:
   - It conceded to Parliament the power to amend any provision of the Constitution, including Fundamental Rights, thereby correcting Golaknath.
   - However, it introduced the Doctrine of Inherent and Implied Limitations: The power to "amend" is not a power to create a new constitution or extinguish the identity of the existing one.
2. Constitutional Identity:
   The majority held that Parliament cannot alter the "Basic Structure". Chief Justice Sikri enumerated illustrative features: Supremacy of the Constitution, Republican and Democratic form, Secularism, Separation of Powers, and Federalism.

IV. CONSOLIDATION THROUGH CRISIS: INDIRA GANDHI, MINERVA MILLS, AND I.R. COELHO
1. Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975 Supp SCC 1):
   When Parliament attempted to validate Indira Gandhi's election by placing it outside judicial review via the 39th Amendment (Article 329A), the Supreme Court struck down the amendment. The Court held that free and fair elections and the rule of law are part of the Basic Structure.
2. Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980 3 SCC 625):
   The 42nd Amendment had introduced clauses (4) and (5) into Article 368, claiming "no limitation whatever" on constituent power. Chief Justice Chandrachud struck down these clauses:
   - "Parliament cannot under Article 368 expand its amending power into an absolute one. The donee of a limited power cannot make itself absolute."
   - The harmony between Part III and Part IV was held to be the bedrock of the Constitution.
3. Waman Rao (1981) and I.R. Coelho (2007):
   The 9-judge bench in I.R. Coelho settled the Ninth Schedule controversy: Any law placed in the Ninth Schedule after 24 April 1973 must pass the "Rights Test" (Articles 14, 19, 21 as basic structure). The Ninth Schedule cannot become a constitutional black hole.
4. NJAC Judgment (2015):
   The Supreme Court invalidated the 99th Amendment, cementing the independence of the judiciary as part of the Basic Structure.

V. PROCEDURAL ANCHOR & LITIGATION CHECKLIST (SENIOR COUNSEL REFERENCE)
1. Exclusive Applicability: Basic Structure can only be invoked to challenge Constitutional Amendments under Article 368, not ordinary legislation (State of A.P. v. McDowell).
2. Judicial Forum: Heard by a 5-judge Constitution Bench under Article 145(3) of the Supreme Court or High Court under Article 226.
3. The Twin Test of Invalidation:
   (a) Does the amendment touch a recognized pillar of the basic structure?
   (b) Does the amendment merely regulate, or does it abrogate, emasculate, and destroy the essence of that pillar (The Essence Test)?

VI. CONCLUSION & CURRENT-LAW MILESTONE
The Basic Structure Doctrine successfully prevented India from slipping into electoral autocracy. By harmonizing parliamentary power with inviolable constitutional values, it ensures that the Constitution remains supreme. Current through the 106th Amendment (2023).
questionsAndAnswers.explanation: Exhaustive CREAC essay covering historical roots, Kesavananda, Indira Gandhi, Minerva Mills, I.R. Coelho, and the NJAC ruling.

questionsAndAnswers.question: What is the cut-off date for judicial review of Ninth Schedule laws under the Basic Structure Doctrine?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: The cut-off date is 24 April 1973 (the date of the Kesavananda Bharati judgment). In Waman Rao (1981) and I.R. Coelho (2007), the Supreme Court ruled that all laws inserted into the Ninth Schedule after 24 April 1973 are subject to judicial review for violation of the Basic Structure.

enhancement.definition: The Basic Structure Doctrine is a judicially crafted constitutional limitation on the constituent power of Parliament under Article 368. First articulated in Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973), it establishes that while Parliament possesses plenary power to amend any provision of the Constitution, it cannot alter, damage, or destroy the core identity and essential framework ('basic structure') of the Constitution.
enhancement.legalPrinciple: The constituent amending power under Article 368 is a power to amend, not to destroy or substitute the Constitution. The Constitution is supreme over Parliament; any constitutional amendment that destroys a basic feature is ultra vires and void.
statutoryFramework: Article 368 of the Constitution of India (Power of Parliament to amend the Constitution)
Article 13 of the Constitution of India (Judicial Review and definition of law)
Formulated by a 13-Judge Constitution Bench in Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) 4 SCC 225
Reaffirmed and expanded in Indira Nehru Gandhi (1975), Minerva Mills (1980), S.R. Bommai (1994), I.R. Coelho (2007), and NJAC Case (2016)
essentialIngredients: Distinction between Constituent Power and Plenary Power: Parliament's amending power under Article 368 is derived from the Constitution; a created body cannot destroy its creator.

Non-Exhaustive Core Features: The basic structure is not rigidly codified but determined on case-by-case adjudication. Recognized features include: Supremacy of the Constitution, Republican and Democratic form of government, Secular character, Separation of Powers, Federalism, Judicial Review, Rule of Law, and Free and Fair Elections.
Threshold of Invalidation: An amendment is invalid only if it damages or emasculates the very identity of the Constitution or a core feature, not merely because it modifies an ordinary provision.
Temporal Cut-off for Ninth Schedule: Laws placed in the Ninth Schedule after 24 April 1973 are open to basic structure scrutiny (I.R. Coelho).
enhancement.detailedExplanation:
The Basic Structure Doctrine emerged from a historic tension between Parliament's drive for absolute amending power and the judiciary's role as guardian of constitutional supremacy.

### The Historical Dialectic
1. **Shankari Prasad v. Union of India (1951) & Sajjan Singh v. State of Rajasthan (1965):** The Supreme Court held that Parliament's amending power under Article 368 was unlimited; 'law' under Article 13(2) referred only to ordinary legislative law, not constitutional amendments.
2. **I.C. Golaknath v. State of Punjab (1967):** An 11-judge bench reversed this position, holding by a 6:5 majority that Parliament could not amend Fundamental Rights, treating constitutional amendments as 'law' under Article 13(2).
3. **24th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1971:** Parliament enacted Article 13(4) and Article 368(3) to expressly bypass Golaknath, asserting absolute amending authority.
4. **Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973):** Overruling Golaknath, the 13-judge bench upheld the 24th Amendment, affirming that Parliament can amend any provision, including Fundamental Rights. However, by a 7:6 majority, the Court held that the power to 'amend' does not include the power to abrogate or destroy the Constitution's 'basic structure'.

### Landmark Applications
- **Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975):** Struck down Article 329A(4) (validating the election of the Prime Minister unconditionally) as destroying Free and Fair Elections and Judicial Review.
- **Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India (1980):** Struck down clauses (4) and (5) of Article 368 (which barred judicial review of amendments and claimed unlimited amending power) because 'a limited amending power is one of the basic features of Indian Constitution'.
- **I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu (2007):** Held that laws placed in the Ninth Schedule after 24 April 1973 are subject to basic structure review if they violate Part III rights.
- **Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Assn. v. Union of India (NJAC Case, 2016):** Struck down the 99th Constitutional Amendment and the NJAC Act for violating the Independence of the Judiciary, an essential facet of the basic structure.
examples: Elimination of Judicial Review: Parliament passes a constitutional amendment inserting a clause that no constitutional amendment shall be called in question in any court on any ground. Applying Minerva Mills, the Supreme Court strikes down the clause as an unconstitutional assault on Judicial Review and the limited nature of amending power.

Electoral Interference: A constitutional amendment alters Article 324 to permit the Union Cabinet to directly appoint party officials to count votes and declare election results without an independent Election Commission. The Supreme Court strikes it down as violative of the basic feature of Free and Fair Elections and Democracy.
distinctions: Basic Structure Review vs Ordinary Judicial Review: Ordinary judicial review tests statutes against specific constitutional provisions; basic structure review tests constitutional amendments against the unwritten foundational principles and identity of the Constitution.

Constituent Power vs Legislative Power: Legislative power is exercised under the Constitution (Articles 245–246) and is subject to Part III; constituent power is exercised to amend the Constitution (Article 368) and is constrained only by the Basic Structure.
problemApplication: Issue: Whether a constitutional amendment establishing a unitary state by dissolving state assemblies and centralizing all legislative power in Parliament violates the Basic Structure Doctrine.
Rule: Federalism is an established basic feature of the Indian Constitution (S.R. Bommai; Kesavananda Bharati). Any amendment abrogating federal power violates the core identity.
Application: By abolishing State Legislatures, the amendment destroys federalism, annihilates dual polity, and converts India into an unconstitutional unitary system.
Counterargument: Parliament argues that Article 368 allows restructuring of governance models based on national security and developmental urgency.
Conclusion: The amendment is ultra vires Article 368 and void ab initio for destroying the basic structure of the Constitution.

Conclusion: The doctrine as the bedrock of constitutional supremacy in India.
sixteenMark: Historical Background: Land reform legislation, Article 31, and the tussle over constituent power.
The Doctrinal Dialectic: Exhaustive analysis of Shankari Prasad, Sajjan Singh, Golaknath, and the 24th/25th Amendments.
Detailed Deconstruction of Kesavananda Bharati: Ratios of Sikri CJ, Hegde, Mukherjea, Shelat, Grover, Jaganmohan Reddy, and Khanna JJ.
Catalogue of Basic Features: Dynamic and evolving list across judicial decisions.
The Minerva Mills Invalidation: Why a limited power cannot expand itself into unlimited constituent authority.
Ninth Schedule and I.R. Coelho: The 'Rights Test' vs the 'Essence of Rights Test'.
Critique & Defense: Democratic legitimacy vs counter-majoritarian protection of constitutionalism.

keyTakeaways: Parliament cannot alter, emasculate, or destroy the Basic Structure under Article 368.
Formulated on 24 April 1973 by a 7:6 majority in Kesavananda Bharati.
Judicial review, federalism, secularism, democracy, and rule of law are non-negotiable basic features.
Post-1973 Ninth Schedule inclusions are fully amenable to basic structure judicial review (I.R. Coelho).
